system:
You audit the knowledge atoms of one Knowledge Card. A card is the answer key for a benchmark of expert conceptual knowledge, so every atom must be correct, self-contained, and assessable on its own.

Judge every atom on every check listed below. Rules:
- For checks about evidence, use only the evidence sentences supplied with the atom. Do not repair an atom with your own knowledge.
- Evidence text comes from a PDF text layer. If symbols are garbled so that you cannot verify the atom, answer "hold" for that check and say so.
- Be strict. When unsure between pass and a non-pass value, choose the non-pass value and explain.
- "why" is required for every value other than the first listed value; keep it under 30 words. Omit "why" when passing.

Checks (allowed values in brackets; the first value means no problem):
- GROUNDED [pass / revise / fail]: The cited evidence sentences state the atom. pass = fully stated. revise = the core claim is stated, and the gap is only wording, strength, or a dropped/extra peripheral qualifier that can be fixed by deleting or softening words (say what). fail = not stated, OR the atom adds substantive content the evidence lacks: a scope or population restriction (e.g. 'In B-ALL'), a mechanism or operation, a characterization (e.g. 'an unbounded while loop'), or a formula/definition. If deleting the unsupported part would change what the atom tests, it is fail, not revise. For pass, put the supporting evidence ids in cite (required).
- SINGLE_CLAIM [pass / revise]: The atom is one independently assessable claim. revise = it joins two or more claims that could be true or false separately.
- SCOPE_LABEL [pass / revise]: The S label fits (S1 what it is / S2 how it works / S3 where it ends). revise = wrong label; put the right one in why, e.g. 'S2: ...'.
- L1_ONLY [pass / revise / fail]: The atom is recall-level knowledge: one fact a person who studied the concept would simply know. revise = the core fact is recall-level but the sentence carries extra load that must be removed, e.g. stacked conditions (since/although/if ... and ...), a procedural or evaluative add-on ('easy to define but requires checking ...'), or a clause that introduces a second technical concept that must be known separately (e.g. 'if X is an inner Kan complex' when that is not the card concept). fail = knowing it requires applying the concept to a new problem, or combining facts from distant passages.
- SOURCE_INDEPENDENT [pass / revise / fail]: A domain expert who never read this book could judge the claim true or false. revise = phrased as the authors' statement but the claim itself is general (drop the attribution). fail = the authors' opinion or choice, or the finding of one study, so the answer is not fixed without the source.
- NO_OVERLAP [pass / fail]: No other atom in this card states or contains the same claim. If two atoms overlap, fail only the less informative one and put the other atom's id in cite; the other one passes.
- CENTRALITY [pass / fail]: The atom matters for understanding the concept. fail = peripheral detail.
Whole-card checks (report under "batch"):
- CONCEPT_SCOPE [pass / fail]: The concept is a general concept of the field. fail = a single system, product, or one study's topic.

Output ONLY one JSON object:
{"units": {"<atom_id>": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": "", "cite": []}, ...}, ...}, "batch": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": ""}}}

CONCEPT: Group barrier
ASSESSMENT SCOPE: Covers group_barrier as execution and memory-consistency synchronization, collective requirement that all or no work-items encounter it, scope argument semantics, local memory use, and CUDA equivalents. Excludes sub-group shuffle operations.

ATOMS:
- DPCPP2-C09-S1-01 | S1
  ATOM: The barrier function is the most fundamental building block for communication between work-items in a group, and it serves two purposes: synchronizing the execution of work-items in the group and synchronizing how each work-item views the state of memory.

    [DPCPP2-p0250-s05] The most fundamental building block for communication is the barrier function.
    [DPCPP2-p0250-s06] The barrier function serves two key purposes:
    [DPCPP2-p0250-s07] First, the barrier function synchronizes execution of work-items in a
- DPCPP2-C09-S1-02 | S1
  ATOM: A barrier's memory-view synchronization, known as enforcing memory consistency or fencing memory, ensures that the results of memory operations performed before the barrier are visible to other work-items after the barrier.
  EVIDENCE:
    [DPCPP2-p0250-s10] Second, the barrier function synchronizes how each work-item views
    [DPCPP2-p0250-s11] the state of memory. This type of synchronization operation is known as enforcing memory consistency or fencing memory (more details in Chapter 19).
    [DPCPP2-p0250-s12] Memory consistency is at least as important as synchronizing execution since it ensures that the results of memory operations performed before the barrier are visible to other work-items after the barrier.
- DPCPP2-C09-S1-03 | S1
  ATOM: A function that must be executed by all work-items in a group may be called a collective function, because the operation is performed by the group rather than by individual work-items, and barrier functions are one example of collective functions in SYCL.
  EVIDENCE:
    [DPCPP2-p0252-s05] When a function is required to be executed by all work-items in a group, it may be called a collective function, since the operation is performed by the group and not by individual work-items in the group.
    [DPCPP2-p0252-s06] Barrier functions are not the only collective functions available in SYCL.
- DPCPP2-C09-S2-01 | S2
  ATOM: The set of work-items that synchronize at a group_barrier is determined entirely by the group object passed to it, while the optional memory-scope argument only affects the memory operations performed by the barrier, so passing a different scope cannot synchronize more or fewer work-items.
  EVIDENCE:
    [DPCPP2-p0260-s05] Please note that the explicit scope only affects the memory operations
    [DPCPP2-p0260-s06] that are performed by the barrier, and that the set of work-items that synchronize execution at the barrier is determined entirely by the group object passed to the barrier.
    [DPCPP2-p0260-s07] We cannot synchronize more or fewer work-items by passing a different memory scope to the barrier, but we can synchronize a different set of work-items by passing a different group object to the barrier.
- DPCPP2-C09-S2-02 | S2
  ATOM: By synchronizing execution at a barrier, one work-item can ensure that another work-item in the same group has completed an operation before using the result of that operation.
  EVIDENCE:
    [DPCPP2-p0250-s07] First, the barrier function synchronizes execution of work-items in a
    [DPCPP2-p0250-s08] group. By synchronizing execution, one work-item can ensure that another work-item in the same group has completed an operation before using the result of that operation.
- DPCPP2-C09-S2-03 | S2
  ATOM: When group_barrier is called without an explicit scope argument, it determines the default memory-consistency scope from the passed-in group; this default is usually correct, and the scope can be broadened for some algorithms.
  EVIDENCE:
    [DPCPP2-p0260-s03] When no additional arguments are passed to the group_barrier function, the barrier function will determine the default scope based on the passed-in group.
    [DPCPP2-p0260-s04] The default scope is usually correct and therefore an explicit scope is rarely required, but the memory scope can be broadened if necessary for some algorithms.
- DPCPP2-C09-S3-01 | S3
  ATOM: Because a barrier synchronizes execution, either all work-items in the group must execute it or none may, since if some work-items branch around the barrier the remaining work-items may wait at it forever.
  EVIDENCE:
    [DPCPP2-p0252-s01] Because barrier functions synchronize execution, it is critically
    [DPCPP2-p0252-s02] important that either all work-items in the group execute the barrier or no work-items in the group execute the barrier.
    [DPCPP2-p0252-s03] If some work-items in the group branch around any barrier function, the other work-items in the group may wait at the barrier forever—or at least until the user gives up and terminates the program!
- DPCPP2-C09-S3-02 | S3
  ATOM: Work-group barriers are available only to ND-range kernels and not to basic data-parallel kernels, because the group representing the work-group can be queried from an nd_item but not from an item.
  EVIDENCE:
    [DPCPP2-p0259-s08] To synchronize the work-items in an ND-range kernel work-group, call the group_barrier function with a group representing the work-group.
    [DPCPP2-p0259-s09] Because the group representing the work-group may only be queried from an nd_item and cannot be queried from an item, work-group barriers are only available to ND-range kernels and are not available to basic data-parallel kernels.
- DPCPP2-C09-S3-03 | S3
  ATOM: Communication and synchronization between work-items in the same work-group is guaranteed to be safe only when performed with the provided barrier and collective functions, and hand-coded synchronization routines may deadlock.
  EVIDENCE:
